output:
Here it is. I left your name and the date as placeholders so you can fill them in before printing.

---

**Kelechi Obi**
**Croydon**

*November 2026*

---

Dear Kelechi,

You said if I was serious, I should put it in writing — a proper letter, not a voice note — and that you'd read it on the train. Fine. You get a letter. It came by post, because a letter is the point, and because I'm not going to pretend I didn't enjoy the excuse.

Let me start with the ask, because it's the smallest thing I'm asking for.

**Thursday 19 November, 6pm. The training partnership in Lewisham. Open evening.**

I will come with you. You'll see the rooms, meet the people who run the training, hear how the year actually works, ask all the awkward money questions out loud to a real person instead of guessing at 11pm, and then we'll go and eat something. You're not being asked to apply for anything. You're not being asked to sign anything. If it's rubbish, tell me it's rubbish and I'll buy you drinks for a year.

That is the entire ask. Everything else below is just the reasons.

---

**You already do this**

You tutored half of Moremi before those exams. You — the guy who spent three nights with a green marker and a cardboard diagram teaching simultaneous equations to nineteen-year-olds who did not want to be taught — got an A in further maths. You tutored my nephew with fractions at Christmas using portions of jollof rice on plates, and that boy is still talking about it two years later. He calls you Uncle Kelechi and he thinks fractions are about food now. That's not a small thing, by the way. That's a child who was handed a rule he couldn't see and you made it visible with rice.

You explain things without making people feel stupid. You know you do that. You did it for half our hostel and you still do it and you don't even notice it's a skill, which is exactly why it is one.

So the honest question isn't "can Kelechi teach maths." The question is "why is Kelechi not already doing it."

---

**What's actually happening at my school**

Peckham. Eleven hundred kids. Since September we've had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups — which means those groups have had somebody in front of them, but not the same somebody, and not somebody who knows them. The kids can feel it. They ask me questions about the work they did with the supply teacher because they don't trust it. They ask me because they know I'll tell them the truth.

Those two Year 9 groups have a proper teacher coming in September. I want it to be you. That's not the only reason to come on the 19th, but it's the reason that keeps me up at night.

---

**How the route works (the bit I had to phone twice to get right)**

It's a salaried route. One year of training. You get paid while you train — you are not on a zero-hours contract doing unpaid observations in a classroom in Tooting on a Tuesday. It starts September 2027, and applications for next September open soon, which is why I'm writing to you now and not in February. If the open evening makes sense to you, the paperwork follows shortly after. If it doesn't, nothing happens and we're still friends.

I'm telling you the timeline because you hate being ambushed by timelines.

---

**The money, honestly, because you won't believe the rest otherwise**

Yes, there's a drop in the first year. A real one. I'm not going to put a number on it here because the number depends on the route and the band, and I'd rather you got the actual figures from the people who pay you at the open evening rather than from me guessing. Ask them the awkward question. Ask it twice. That's what the evening is for, and they'll respect you for asking, because you're a quantity surveyor — you check other people's numbers for a living, you'd be doing it in a new costume.

What I'll tell you is what comes with it: school holidays, roughly six weeks of the year, paid, plus the bank holidays that aren't school holidays, which is a lot more time than you have now, and none of it requires a spreadsheet. A pension that's one of the better ones in this country. And it goes up — every year, on the scale, and maths is on the list where they actually need people, which is one of the few industries where being needed is worth money. By the time you're properly on the scale it's a different conversation from year one.

But yes. Year one hurts in the wallet. I'm not going to dress it up.

---

**The good part**

Last month a Year 11 boy called Damola finally got simultaneous equations. Three weeks. Three weeks of me not giving up on him while the rest of the class had long since understood it and were getting bored waiting.

And when he finally got it, he looked up and said, *"Is that all??"*

And the whole class clapped.

I've been teaching for seven years and that moment is still the best thing that's ever happened to me. Not the ones who were already good. The one who finally got it and couldn't believe it was allowed to.

That's the job, Kelechi. That specific moment, over and over, three weeks at a time.

---

**The bad part, since you'd only believe the good part if I gave you this one**

Marking is endless. Genuinely endless. There is no version of this where you are finished by six o'clock. There is coursework, data, lesson plans, the paperwork that no one warns you about, and a laptop open at 9pm that you resent.

Some days behaviour is wahala. Some days a class doesn't want you in the room and you go home and think about the fifteen-minute bit where it all went sideways. Some days you teach a lesson and nothing lands and you go home and think about the three things you could have done differently.

And I'm not going to lie about this next one: my first term, in 2019, I cried in the car park twice. Twice. I sat in the car with the engine off because I thought I'd made a mistake coming into teaching. I didn't make a mistake. It just takes a term to find your footing, and then it gets better, and then one day you can't imagine doing anything else. But I did cry, and I'm telling you because you asked for the truth and because you'll respect me more for it.

---

**Before 40**

On your last birthday, in front of your food, you said: *"I just want to do something that matters before 40."*

I'm not going to let that sentence sit in a memory where it does nothing.

You're 34. You've got six years. If you start in September 2027, you'll be 35 when you walk into your first classroom properly, which means you get a whole decade of teaching in front of you before you turn 40. Not six years of it. Ten.

Nine years at the same firm, Kelechi. Nine years of checking other people's costings. I've seen what that does to people — you become a very expensive proofreader for somebody else's budget. You're not auditing the national grid, calm down. You're reading spreadsheets that other people made, on work that somebody else will still be doing long after you've gone.

You are patient. You are funny. Kids would love you, and more than that, they'd remember you, which is a strange thing to say about a job but it's true. My Year 9s still quote things I said in 2021. They quote them at me. It's embarrassing. You would be worse than me, because you were funnier at Unilag.

And for the record — you keep saying you're too old. There's a woman in my department who started teaching at 41. She's the one the Year 11s ask for by name.

---

**What I actually want from you**

Come to the open evening. That's it. 19 November, 6pm, Lewisham.

I'll work out the route from Croydon and send you the timings, and I'll meet you outside Lewisham station so we can go in together — that way you don't have to walk in alone and talk to strangers, which I know is not your favourite thing even though you're better at it than you think.

Bring questions. Bring a notebook if you want. Bring the doubts — all of them, the money one, the age one, the "is my maths still good enough" one, especially that one. We'll go through them. I'll answer the ones I know and we'll find someone who knows the rest.

Afterwards, food. Something proper. Then you go home and think about it for six weeks, and if the answer is no, the answer is no and I'll still be your mate and we'll still complain about the government together.

But I don't think the answer's going to be no. I think you're going to walk into that room on the 19th and I'm going to watch you do that thing where you start talking to a Year 9 and put your head slightly on one side like you used to in Moremi, and I'm going to think: *abeg, why wait another three years.*

One evening. No forms. No commitment.

Come.

**Your mate,**
*[Your name]*

---

**P.S.** If you post me back a voice note saying "I've read it, let's discuss," I will be extremely disappointed and also I will have booked the table for after 7:30 anyway. That's how this works now.

**P.P.S.** The jollof fractions worked. I have thought about that Christmas for two years. Whatever else you do, keep doing that.
